# AF 第七章 原文（重制基线）

## Chapter 7

[P01] It was a very cold winter. First came storms, then sleet（雨夹雪） and snow, and then a hard frost（霜） that lasted into February. The animals worked hard to rebuild the windmill（风车）. They knew the outside world was watching. They knew jealous people would cheer if the mill（磨坊） was not finished on time. Out of spite（恶意）, the humans said they did not believe Snowball had destroyed the windmill. They said it fell because the walls were too thin. The animals knew this was not true.

[P02] But this time they decided to build the walls three feet thick, not eighteen inches as before. This meant they needed much more stone. For a long time, snowdrifts（雪堆） filled the quarry（采石场）, so no work could be done. They made some progress in the dry, frosty（霜冷的） weather that came next. But it was hard work, and the animals did not feel as hopeful（有希望） as before. They were always cold and often hungry too. Only Boxer and Clover never lost hope. Squealer gave fine speeches about the joy of service and the honour of work. But the other animals found more strength in Boxer's power and his never-failing cry of "I will work harder!" In January, food ran short.

[P03] The corn ration（配给） was cut very much. The animals were told they would get extra（额外） potatoes instead. But then they found that most of the potato crop had been frosted（结霜的） in the clamps（夹子）. The clamps had not been covered thickly enough. The potatoes had gone soft and changed colour. Only a few could be eaten. For days at a time the animals had nothing to eat but chaff（谷壳） and mangels（饲料甜菜）. Starvation（饥饿） seemed to stare（盯着） them in the face. It was vitally（至关重要） necessary to hide this fact from the outside world.

[P04] The people became bold after the windmill fell. They made up lies about Animal Farm. They said the animals were dying（垂死） of hunger and disease. They said the animals fought and even ate their own kind. Napoleon knew this was bad. If people knew the truth about the food, it would be worse. He decided to use Mr. Whymper to spread a different idea. Before, the animals had little contact with Whymper on his weekly visits. Now, a few chosen animals, mostly sheep, were told to say in a casual（随意的） way, where he could hear, that rations（配给） had been increased.

[P05] Also, Napoleon told them to fill the almost empty（空的） grain（谷物） bins in the store-shed with sand, nearly to the top. Then they covered the sand with the little grain and meal left. They used a false reason to lead Whymper through the store-shed, letting him see the bins for a moment. He believed it, and kept telling the outside world that there was no food shortage on Animal Farm. Still, by the end of January it was clear they must get more grain from somewhere. These days Napoleon seldom came out in public. He stayed in the farmhouse（农舍）, with fierce dogs guarding every door.

[P06] When he came out, it was a formal event, with six dogs close around him who growled（咆哮） if anyone came too near. Often he did not even appear on Sunday mornings, but gave his orders through another pig, usually Squealer. One Sunday morning Squealer said that the hens, who had just started laying again, must give up their eggs. Napoleon had agreed to a contract through Whymper for four hundred eggs a week. The money would pay for enough grain and meal to keep the farm going until summer. When the hens heard this, they made a terrible outcry（抗议）.

[P07] They had been warned before that they might have to give this up, but did not think it would really happen. They were just getting their nests ready for the spring sitting, and said taking the eggs away now was murder. For the first time since Jones was driven out, something like a revolt（反抗） appeared. Led by three young Black Minorca（米诺卡鸡） pullets（小母鸡）, the hens tried hard to stop Napoleon's wishes. Their way was to fly up to the rafters（椽子） and lay their eggs there, and the eggs broke on the floor. Napoleon acted fast and without pity. He ordered the hens to get no food, and said any animal who gave even one grain of corn to a hen must die.

[P08] The dogs made sure these orders happened. For five days the hens held out, then they gave in and went back to their nesting boxes. Nine hens had died before this. Their bodies were buried in the orchard（果园）, and it was said they died of coccidiosis（球虫病）. Whymper heard nothing of this business, and the eggs were delivered（递送） on time, a grocer（杂货商）'s van（货车） driving up to the farm once a week to take them away.

[P09] People said he was hiding on a nearby farm, either Foxwood（狐林） or Pinchfield（窄地）. By this time Napoleon was on better terms with the other farmers. There was a pile of timber（木材） in the yard, stacked（堆叠） there ten years earlier when a beech（山毛榉） spinney（小树林） was cleared. It was well seasoned, and Whymper had advised Napoleon to sell it to Mr. Pilkington or Mr. Frederick. Both Mr. Pilkington and Mr. Frederick wanted to buy it. Napoleon could not decide between the two. People noticed that whenever he seemed about to agree with Frederick, Snowball was said to be at Foxwood（狐林）, and when he leaned toward Pilkington, Snowball was said to be at Pinchfield（窄地）. Suddenly, early in the spring, a worrying thing was discovered.

[P10] Snowball was secretly visiting the farm at night! The animals were so worried that they could hardly sleep. Every night, they said, he came in quietly and did bad things. He stole the corn, knocked over the milk-pails（桶）, broke the eggs, walked on the seedbeds（苗床）, and bit the bark off the fruit trees. Whenever anything went wrong, they blamed（责备） Snowball. If a window was broken or a drain（排水） was blocked, someone would say Snowball did it. When the key of the store-shed was lost, the whole farm believed Snowball threw it down the well.

[P11] Strangely, they still believed this even after the lost key was found under a sack（麻袋） of meal. The cows all said together that Snowball came into their stalls（畜栏） and milked them while they slept. The rats, which had been a problem that winter, were also said to be working with Snowball. Napoleon ordered a full check into Snowball's acts. With his dogs beside him, he went and made a careful tour of the farm buildings. The other animals followed far behind.

[P12] Napoleon stopped every few steps and snuffed（嗅） the ground for traces（痕迹） of Snowball's footsteps. He said he could find them by the smell. He snuffed in every corner — in the barn（谷仓）, in the cow-shed, in the henhouses（鸡舍）, in the vegetable garden — and found traces of Snowball almost everywhere. He would put his snout（口鼻部） to the ground, give several deep sniffs（嗅）, and cry out in a terrible voice, "Snowball! He has been here! I can smell him distinctly（清楚地）!" At the word "Snowball" all the dogs let out terrible growls（咆哮） and showed their side teeth. The animals were very frightened. It seemed to them that Snowball was some kind of invisible（看不见的） power, filling the air around them and threatening（威胁的） them with all kinds of dangers.

[P13] In the evening Squealer called them together. His face looked worried, and he said he had serious news. "Comrades（同志们）!" cried Squealer, making little nervous jumps. cried Squealer, making little nervous skips, "A most terrible thing has been discovered. Snowball has sold himself to Frederick of Pinchfield Farm. Frederick is planning to attack us and take our farm away! Snowball will act as his guide. But there is worse. We thought Snowball's uprising（起义） was caused by his vanity（虚荣） and ambition. But we were wrong, comrades（同志们）. Do you know the real reason?"

[P14] Snowball worked with Jones from the very start! He was Jones's secret helper all the time. Papers he left behind prove it, and we have only just found them. To my mind this explains a lot, comrades. Did we not see how he tried—but luckily failed—to make us lose and be destroyed at the Battle of the Cowshed（牛棚）?"

The animals were shocked. This was even worse than Snowball destroying the windmill. But it took them some minutes to fully understand. They all remembered how Snowball had run ahead of them at the Battle of the Cowshed（牛棚）, how he had cheered them at every turn, and how he had not stopped even when the pellets（颗粒） from Jones's gun had hurt his back.

[P15] At first it was hard to see how this fit in with his being on Jones's side. Even Boxer, who seldom asked questions, was puzzled（困惑）. He lay down, tucked（塞进） his fore（前部） hoofs（蹄） under him, shut his eyes, and tried hard to think. "I do not believe that," he said. "Snowball fought bravely at the Battle of the Cowshed. I saw him myself. Did we not give him 'Animal Hero, first Class,' right after?" "That was our mistake, comrade（同志）. We know now—it is all written in the secret papers we have found—that he was really trying to lead us to our doom（厄运）." "But he was wounded," said Boxer.

[P16] "We all saw him running with blood." "That was part of the plan!" cried Squealer. "Jones's shot only grazed（放牧） him. I could show you this in his own writing. The plan was for Snowball, at the key moment, to give the signal（信号） to run away and leave the field to the enemy. He almost did it -- in fact, comrades, he WOULD have done it if our heroic（英勇） Leader, Comrade Napoleon, had not stopped him. Don't（不） you remember how, when Jones and his men got inside the yard, Snowball suddenly turned and ran, and many animals followed him?

[P17] And do you not remember, too, that just then, when panic was spreading and all seemed lost, Comrade Napoleon jumped forward, crying 'Death to Humanity（人类）!' and bit Jones's leg? Surely you remember THAT, comrades?" cried Squealer, jumping from side to side. Now when Squealer told the story so clearly, it seemed to the animals that they did remember it. At least, they remembered that at the key moment of the battle Snowball had turned to run away. But Boxer was still a little worried. "I do not believe Snowball was a traitor at the start," he said at last.

[P18] "What he did after is different. But at the Battle of the Cowshed, our Leader, Comrade Napoleon, was a good comrade."Our Leader, Comrade Napoleon," said Squealer, slowly and firmly, "has said clearly that Snowball was Jones's agent from the very start—long before anyone thought of the uprising." "Ah, that is different!" said Boxer. "If Comrade Napoleon says it, it must be right." "That is the true spirit, comrade!" cried Squealer, but the animals noticed he gave Boxer an ugly look with his little twinkling（闪烁） eyes. He turned to go, then stopped and added, "I warn every animal to keep his eyes wide open."

[P19] For we have reason to think that some of Snowball's secret agents are hiding among us right now!" Four days later, in the late afternoon, Napoleon ordered all the animals to come together in the yard. When they were all there, Napoleon came out of the farmhouse. He wore both his medals (for he had recently given himself "Animal Hero, First Class" and "Animal Hero, Second Class"). His nine huge dogs jumped around him and made low sounds that made all the animals shake with fear. They all bent down silently. They seemed to know that some terrible thing was about to happen. Napoleon stood sternly（严厉地） looking over his audience; then he made a high-pitched（投掷） cry.

[P20] Right away the dogs ran forward. Immediately, they caught four pigs by the ear and pulled them, squealing with pain, to Napoleon's feet. The pigs' ears were bleeding. The dogs had tasted blood and seemed to go mad. Three of them threw themselves upon Boxer. Boxer put out his great hoof（蹄）, caught a dog in mid-air, and pinned（固定） him to the ground. The dog shrieked（尖叫） for mercy（仁慈）, and the other two ran away. Boxer looked at Napoleon to know whether he should crush（压碎） the dog or let it go.

[P21] Napoleon sharply（尖锐地） ordered Boxer to let the dog go. Boxer lifted his hoof, and the hurt dog ran off crying. Soon the noise died down. The four pigs waited, shaking, their faces full of guilt（罪行）. Napoleon called on them to confess（坦白） their crimes. These were the same four pigs who had protested（抗议） when Napoleon ended the Sunday Meetings. They confessed（坦白） they had been in touch with Snowball since he was driven out, had helped him destroy the windmill, and had agreed to hand over Animal Farm to Mr.

[P22] Frederick. They also said Snowball had told them in secret that he had been Jones's spy（间谍） for many years. After they finished, the dogs quickly tore out their throats. In a terrible voice Napoleon asked if any other animal had something to confess. The three hens who had led the uprising over the eggs came forward. They said Snowball had come to them in a dream and told them to disobey（违抗） Napoleon. They were killed too. Then a goose came forward and said she had hidden six ears of corn during the last harvest and eaten them at night.

[P23] Then a sheep admitted（承认） she had made the drinking water dirty—she said Snowball pushed her to do it. Two other sheep admitted they killed an old ram（公羊）, a loyal（忠诚） follower of Napoleon, by running after him around a fire when he had a bad cough. All were killed right there. So the confessions（坦白） and killings（杀戮） went on, until a pile of dead bodies lay at Napoleon's feet and the air smelled strongly of blood. Since Jones was driven out, no one had smelled blood like that. When it was over, the other animals, all except the pigs and dogs, crept（爬行） away together.

[P24] They were shaken and miserable（悲惨的）. They did not know which was more shocking—the treachery（背叛） of the animals who had joined Snowball, or the cruel retribution（报应） they had just seen. In the old days there had often been bloody（血腥） scenes just as terrible, but it seemed far worse now that it was happening among themselves. Since Jones had left, no animal had killed another animal. They made their way to the little knoll（小丘） where the half-finished windmill stood, and all lay down as though huddling（挤在一起） for warmth（温暖）—Clover, Muriel, Benjamin, the cows, the sheep, and a whole flock（羊群） of geese and hens—everyone except the cat, who had suddenly disappeared just before Napoleon ordered the animals to assemble（集合）.

[P25] For a while nobody spoke. Only Boxer stayed on his feet. He moved to and fro（来回）, and now and then he gave a little whinny（嘶鸣） of surprise. At last he said: "I do not understand it. I would not have believed that such things could happen on our farm. It must be due（由于） to some fault in ourselves. The solution is to work harder. From now onwards（向前） I shall get up a full hour earlier in the mornings." And he moved off at his heavy trot（疾走） and made for the quarry.

[P26] After he got there, he picked up two loads（负载） of stone and pulled them to the windmill before he stopped for the night. The animals crowded around Clover and said nothing. From the small hill, they could see most of Animal Farm—the long grass field, the hay（干草） field, the small wood, the drinking pool, the wheat fields, and the red roofs with smoke from the chimneys（烟囱）. It was a clear spring evening. The grass and hedges（树篱）, full of new buds（芽）, were turned gold by the low sun.

[P27] The farm had never looked so lovely. They remembered with surprise it was their own farm—all of it belonged to them. Clover looked down the hill, her eyes full of tears. If she could speak, she would say this was not what they wanted. They had worked years ago to bring down humans, but not for these terrible, bloody scenes on the night old Major first moved them to rise up. Her picture of the future was a society of animals free from hunger and the whip, all equal, each working as he could, the strong protecting the weak—as she had protected the lost baby ducks with her leg on the night of Major's speech.

[P28] Instead, she did not know why they had come to a time when no one dared speak his mind, when fierce, growling dogs roamed everywhere, and when friends were torn to pieces after they said they had done shocking crimes. She did not think of uprising. She knew that even now they were much better off than in the days of Jones, and that they must stop the humans from coming back. Whatever happened, she would stay faithful, work hard, do her orders, and accept Napoleon as leader.

[P29] But still, this was not what she and the other animals had hoped and worked for. This was not why they had built the windmill and faced the bullets（子弹） from Jones's gun. These were her thoughts, but she did not have the words to say them. At last, feeling that singing was somehow（不知怎的） a substitute（替代） for the words she could not find, she began to sing "Beasts（野兽） of England." The other animals sitting round her joined in, and they sang it three times over—very tunefully（悦耳地）, but slowly and mournfully（悲伤）, in a way they had never sung it before. They had just finished singing it for the third time when Squealer, with two dogs, came up to them, looking as if he had something important to say.

[P30] He told them that, by a special order of Comrade Napoleon, "Beasts（野兽） of England" was abolished（废除）. From then on, no one could sing it. The animals were shocked. "Why?" cried Muriel. "It is not needed any more, comrade," said Squealer coldly. "'Beasts of England' was the song of the rebellion（造反）. But the rebellion is finished now. The killing of the traitors this afternoon was the last act. The enemy outside and inside has been beaten. In 'Beasts of England' we showed our wish for a better society. But that society has now been built. Clearly this song has no purpose any more." The animals were afraid, and some might have argued, but just then the sheep began their usual bleating of "Four legs good, two legs bad," which lasted several minutes and ended the talk. So "Beasts of England" was heard no more.

[P31] Then Minimus the poet wrote another song. It began: Animal Farm, Animal Farm, Never through me shall you come to harm! The animals sang it every Sunday morning after they raised the flag. But somehow the words and the tune never seemed as good to them as 'Beasts of England'.
